claim: IgE is the least abundant circulating antibody class but is constitutively present in healthy tissues bound to resident cells via its high-affinity receptor, FcεRI.
source: IgE is the least abundant circulating antibody class but is constitutively present in healthy tissues bound to resident cells via its high-affinity receptor, FcεRI.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about IgE biology.

claim: Skin inflammation enhances levels of IgE antibodies that have natural specificities and a repertoire, VDJ rearrangements and CDRH3 characteristics similar to those of IgE antibodies in healthy tissue.
source: Here we show, in mice, that skin inflammation enhances levels of IgE antibodies that have natural specificities and a repertoire, VDJ rearrangements and CDRH3 characteristics similar to those of IgE antibodies in healthy tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by high-throughput sequencing data presented in Figure 2 showing VDJ usage and CDRH3 characteristics.

claim: IgE-bearing basophils are recruited to inflamed skin via CXCL12 and thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP)/IL-3-dependent upregulation of CXCR4.
source: IgE-bearing basophils are recruited to inflamed skin via CXCL12 and thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP)/IL-3-dependent upregulation of CXCR4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing CXCR4 upregulation and blocking experiments.

claim: IgE/FcεRI-signalling in basophils promotes epithelial cell growth and differentiation, partly through histamine engagement of H1R and H4R.
source: In the inflamed skin, IgE/FcεRI-signalling in basophils promotes epithelial cell growth and differentiation, partly through histamine engagement of H1R and H4R.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro keratinocyte culture experiments and receptor blocking studies shown in Figure 5.

claim: The IgE response strongly drives tumour outgrowth of epithelial cells harbouring oncogenic mutation.
source: Furthermore, this IgE response strongly drives tumour outgrowth of epithelial cells harbouring oncogenic mutation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by DMBA-TPA carcinogenesis experiments in IgE-deficient mice shown in Figure 3.

claim: Natural IgE antibodies support skin barrier defences, but during chronic tissue inflammation this role may be subverted to promote tumour growth.
source: These findings indicate that natural IgE antibodies support skin barrier defences, but that during chronic tissue inflammation this role may be subverted to promote tumour growth.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data showing both protective and tumor-promoting roles.

claim: IgE is present at low concentrations in the blood.
source: IgE is present at low concentrations in the blood and is the least abundant circulating antibody class.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about IgE.

claim: All epithelial tissues contain resident cells constitutively binding IgE antibodies.
source: However, all epithelial tissues contain resident cells constitutively binding IgE antibodies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The half-life of free IgE in the serum is short (1–2 days).
source: Although the half-life of free IgE in the serum is short (1–2 days), tissue-resident IgE may persists for weeks or months (Geha et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Geha et al., 2003.

claim: Tissue-resident IgE may persist for weeks or months.
source: Although the half-life of free IgE in the serum is short (1–2 days), tissue-resident IgE may persists for weeks or months (Geha et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Geha et al., 2003.

claim: IgE is bound with high affinity to its receptor, FcεRI, in tissue.
source: In the tissue, IgE is bound with high affinity to its receptor, FcεRI, and can remain bound for the life of the FcεRI-bearing cell (MacGlashan, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to MacGlashan, 2008.

claim: IgE can remain bound to FcεRI for the life of the FcεRI-bearing cell.
source: In the tissue, IgE is bound with high affinity to its receptor, FcεRI, and can remain bound for the life of the FcεRI-bearing cell (MacGlashan, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to MacGlashan, 2008.

claim: Spontaneous production of natural IgE has been suggested to be a component of innate tissue defence.
source: The specificity and function of this endogenous IgE in healthy individuals is unclear, although spontaneous production of natural IgE has been suggested to be a component of innate tissue defence (McCoy et al., 2006; Palm et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McCoy et al., 2006 and Palm et al., 2012.

claim: Mast cells and basophils are the only two cell types that express the complete high-affinity receptor for IgE (FcεRI) with all four polypeptide subunits (αβγ2).
source: Mast cells and basophils are the only two cell types that express the complete high-affinity receptor for IgE (FcεRI) with all four polypeptide subunits (αβγ2).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about FcεRI expression.

claim: In humans, subsets of dendritic cells, monocytes and eosinophils can express low levels of FcεRI but only as a trimer, lacking the β chain (αγ2).
source: In humans, subsets of dendritic cells, monocytes and eosinophils can express low levels of FcεRI but only as a trimer, lacking the β chain (αγ2).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about FcεRI expression in humans.

claim: The density of mast cell and basophil FcεR1 expression correlates with serum IgE levels.
source: The density of mast cell and basophil FcεR1 expression correlates with serum IgE levels, so an increase in IgE antibody may directly increase FcεRI signalling (Lawrence et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lawrence et al., 2017.

claim: An increase in IgE antibody may directly increase FcεRI signalling.
source: The density of mast cell and basophil FcεR1 expression correlates with serum IgE levels, so an increase in IgE antibody may directly increase FcεRI signalling (Lawrence et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between IgE levels and FcεRI expression, supported by citation.

claim: Paul Ehrlich first described mast cells and basophils in 1878.
source: Paul Ehrlich first described mast cells and basophils in 1878, and estimated that there were enough mast cells in the body to make up 'an organ the size of the spleen' (Crivellato et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation to Crivellato et al., 2003.

claim: Mast cells are constitutively resident in tissues, such as the skin.
source: Mast cells are constitutively resident in tissues, such as the skin, whereas basophils are circulating cells that rapidly infiltrate inflamed tissues.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mast cell and basophil biology.

claim: Basophils are circulating cells that rapidly infiltrate inflamed tissues.
source: Mast cells are constitutively resident in tissues, such as the skin, whereas basophils are circulating cells that rapidly infiltrate inflamed tissues.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about basophil biology.

claim: Crosslinking of FcεRI-bound IgE on mast cells and basophils causes degranulation and immediate release of potent pharmacologically active pre-formed mediators.
source: Crosslinking of FcεRI-bound IgE on these cells causes degranulation and immediate release of potent pharmacologically active pre-formed mediators and concurrent synthesis of cytokines/chemokines and inflammatory lipid mediators.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about FcεRI signaling.

claim: Crosslinking of FcεRI-bound IgE causes concurrent synthesis of cytokines/chemokines and inflammatory lipid mediators.
source: Crosslinking of FcεRI-bound IgE on these cells causes degranulation and immediate release of potent pharmacologically active pre-formed mediators and concurrent synthesis of cytokines/chemokines and inflammatory lipid mediators.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about FcεRI signaling.

claim: Mast cells and basophils mediate a 'gate-keeper' function and promote barrier defences at the skin and mucosal surfaces.
source: Although the in vivo role(s) of both cell types is only partially understood, it has been suggested that they mediate a 'gate-keeper' function and promote barrier defences at the skin and mucosal surfaces (Voehringer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Voehringer, 2013.

claim: IgE antibodies play an important protective role in host defence against noxious environmental substances such as venoms, hematophagous fluids, environmental xenobiotics and irritants.
source: However, it has been proposed that they also play an important protective role in host defence against noxious environmental substances such as venoms, hematophagous fluids, environmental xenobiotics and irritants (Palm et al., 2012; Profet, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Palm et al., 2012 and Profet, 1991.

claim: Topical exposure to environmental carcinogens promotes potent de novo induction of autoreactive IgE antibodies.
source: In support of this, we recently demonstrated that topical exposure to environmental carcinogens promotes potent de novo induction of autoreactive IgE antibodies, and that these IgE antibodies provide protection against epithelial carcinogenesis in the exposed tissue (Crawford et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crawford et al., 2018.

claim: Carcinogen-induced IgE antibodies provide protection against epithelial carcinogenesis in the exposed tissue.
source: In support of this, we recently demonstrated that topical exposure to environmental carcinogens promotes potent de novo induction of autoreactive IgE antibodies, and that these IgE antibodies provide protection against epithelial carcinogenesis in the exposed tissue (Crawford et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crawford et al., 2018.

claim: The induction of IgE by carcinogens was dependent on epithelial cell DNA-damage.
source: The induction of IgE was dependent on epithelial cell (EC) DNA-damage, and deep-sequencing of these IgE antibodies revealed that they have a unique repertoire with specific VDJ rearrangements and CDRH3 characteristics that are distinct from those of IgE produced during general tissue inflammation (Crawford et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crawford et al., 2018.

claim: Carcinogen-induced IgE antibodies have a unique repertoire with specific VDJ rearrangements and CDRH3 characteristics that are distinct from those of IgE produced during general tissue inflammation.
source: The induction of IgE was dependent on epithelial cell (EC) DNA-damage, and deep-sequencing of these IgE antibodies revealed that they have a unique repertoire with specific VDJ rearrangements and CDRH3 characteristics that are distinct from those of IgE produced during general tissue inflammation (Crawford et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crawford et al., 2018.

claim: Epidermal hyperplasia and inflammation are hallmarks of a wide range of skin conditions.
source: Epidermal hyperplasia and inflammation are hallmarks of a wide range of skin conditions.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about skin pathology.

claim: Chronic inflammation may aid the proliferation and survival of epithelial cells harbouring genomic alterations.
source: Furthermore, chronic inflammation may aid the proliferation and survival of EC harbouring genomic alterations, and so is now widely accepted to promote cancer development (Mantovani et al., 2008; Coussens et al., 2013; Grivennikov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mantovani et al., 2008; Coussens et al., 2013; Grivennikov et al., 2010.

claim: Chronic inflammation is now widely accepted to promote cancer development.
source: Furthermore, chronic inflammation may aid the proliferation and survival of EC harbouring genomic alterations, and so is now widely accepted to promote cancer development (Mantovani et al., 2008; Coussens et al., 2013; Grivennikov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mantovani et al., 2008; Coussens et al., 2013; Grivennikov et al., 2010.

claim: General tissue inflammation enhances the levels of polyclonal natural IgE with similar characteristics and VDJ usage as IgE in naïve animals.
source: We show that general tissue inflammation enhances the levels of polyclonal natural IgE with similar characteristics and VDJ usage as IgE in naïve animals.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data in Figure 2.

claim: IgE, via FcεRI-signalling in basophils, potently promotes epidermal hyperplasia.
source: Furthermore, this IgE, via FcεRI-signalling in basophils, potently promotes epidermal hyperplasia and inflammation-driven outgrowth of skin tumours following subclinical carcinogen exposure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: IgE promotes inflammation-driven outgrowth of skin tumours following subclinical carcinogen exposure.
source: Furthermore, this IgE, via FcεRI-signalling in basophils, potently promotes epidermal hyperplasia and inflammation-driven outgrowth of skin tumours following subclinical carcinogen exposure.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Tissue inflammation recruits IgE-bearing basophils to the skin via CXCL12.
source: Tissue inflammation recruits IgE-bearing basophils to the skin via CXCL12 and TSLP/IL-3-dependent upregulation of CXCR4 on circulating basophils.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: TSLP/IL-3 upregulates CXCR4 on circulating basophils.
source: Tissue inflammation recruits IgE-bearing basophils to the skin via CXCL12 and TSLP/IL-3-dependent upregulation of CXCR4 on circulating basophils.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: IgE-dependent basophil degranulation in the skin supports epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation, partly via histamine.
source: IgE-dependent basophil degranulation in the skin supports EC proliferation and differentiation, partly via histamine.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Resting healthy murine skin contains large amounts of IgE despite very low levels in serum.
source: Consistent with this, a horizontal view of resting healthy murine skin revealed that large amounts of IgE was normally present in the tissue (Figure 1a) despite very low levels in serum (Figure 1b–d).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1a and ELISA data in Figure 1b-d.

claim: IgE in resting skin is mainly found on cells around the hair-follicles.
source: IgE in resting skin was mainly found on cells around the hair-follicles (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1a.

claim: Topical exposure to TPA significantly enhances circulating levels of IgE compared to untreated or vehicle-treated animals.
source: Topical exposure to agents that induce skin inflammation, such as 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate (TPA, a protein kinase C activator) (Figure 1b), MC903 (a vitamin D3 analogue commonly used to induce atopic dermatitis-like inflammation) (Figure 1c) and R848 (resiquimod, a toll-like receptor seven agonist commonly used to induce psoriasis-like inflammation) (Figure 1d), significantly enhanced the circulating levels of IgE compared to those in untreated or vehicle-treated animals.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 1b.

claim: Topical exposure to MC903 significantly enhances circulating levels of IgE compared to untreated or vehicle-treated animals.
source: Topical exposure to agents that induce skin inflammation, such as 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate (TPA, a protein kinase C activator) (Figure 1b), MC903 (a vitamin D3 analogue commonly used to induce atopic dermatitis-like inflammation) (Figure 1c) and R848 (resiquimod, a toll-like receptor seven agonist commonly used to induce psoriasis-like inflammation) (Figure 1d), significantly enhanced the circulating levels of IgE compared to those in untreated or vehicle-treated animals.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 1c.

claim: Topical exposure to R848 significantly enhances circulating levels of IgE compared to untreated or vehicle-treated animals.
source: Topical exposure to agents that induce skin inflammation, such as 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate (TPA, a protein kinase C activator) (Figure 1b), MC903 (a vitamin D3 analogue commonly used to induce atopic dermatitis-like inflammation) (Figure 1c) and R848 (resiquimod, a toll-like receptor seven agonist commonly used to induce psoriasis-like inflammation) (Figure 1d), significantly enhanced the circulating levels of IgE compared to those in untreated or vehicle-treated animals.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 1d.

claim: Enhancement of serum IgE is dependent on topical exposure; intravenous or intraperitoneal administration does not trigger the same effect.
source: Enhancement of serum IgE was dependent on topical exposure: intravenous (i.v.) or intraperitoneal (i.p.) administration did not trigger the same effect, as shown by R848 exposure (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 1d comparing different routes of administration.

claim: The increase in serum IgE is accompanied by an increase in the number of IgE-secreting plasma cells in the skin-draining lymph nodes.
source: The increase in serum IgE was accompanied by an increase in the number of IgE-secreting plasma cells in the skin-draining lymph nodes (LNs) (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 1e,f.

claim: IgE levels are increased locally in the skin following topical TPA treatment.
source: IgE levels were also increased locally in the skin following topical TPA treatment (Figure 1g), but most notably the cells carrying the IgE switched from being predominantly mast cells in resting untreated skin to mainly basophils in TPA-treated inflamed skin (Figure 1h,i).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1g.

claim: The cells carrying IgE switch from being predominantly mast cells in resting untreated skin to mainly basophils in TPA-treated inflamed skin.
source: IgE levels were also increased locally in the skin following topical TPA treatment (Figure 1g), but most notably the cells carrying the IgE switched from being predominantly mast cells in resting untreated skin to mainly basophils in TPA-treated inflamed skin (Figure 1h,i).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 1h,i.

claim: 24 hr after cessation of TPA treatment, only a few mast cells remain in the skin, while IgE-bearing basophils account for ~2% of total CD45+ leukocytes.
source: 24 hr after cessation of TPA treatment, only a few mast cells remained in the skin, while IgE-bearing basophils accounted for ~2% of total CD45+ leukocytes.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 1i.

claim: Basophil numbers increase at 48 hr after cessation of TPA treatment and then decline as the inflammation subsides, while mast cells return to the skin.
source: Basophil numbers further increased at 48 hr after cessation of TPA treatment and then declined as the inflammation subsided, while mast cells returned to the skin (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 1i showing time course.

claim: The IgE repertoire in TPA-treated mice is highly diverse and polyclonal with ~75% of the repertoire consisting of clone sizes ≤ 10.
source: To understand the nature of IgE-induced during skin inflammation, we performed high-throughput sequencing of the IgE heavy-chain repertoire from mice exposed topically to TPA. This revealed the repertoires to be highly diverse and polyclonal with ~75% of the repertoire consisting of clone sizes ≤ 10 (Figure 2a), which was similar to that seen in untreated naïve mice.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data in Figure 2a.

claim: The IgE repertoire in TPA-treated mice is similar to that seen in untreated naïve mice, suggesting that no notable selection or clonal expansion had occurred.
source: This revealed the repertoires to be highly diverse and polyclonal with ~75% of the repertoire consisting of clone sizes ≤ 10 (Figure 2a), which was similar to that seen in untreated naïve mice. This suggests that no notable selection or clonal expansion had occurred.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequencing data in Figure 2a.

claim: IgHV1 is the most dominant Igh-V family gene, accounting for >70% of the IgE repertoire.
source: Thus, we analysed the use of genes encoding the variable, diversity and joining (VDJ) regions of the IgE heavy-chain and found that IgHV1 was the most dominant Igh-V family gene, accounting for >70% of the repertoire (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data in Figure 2b.

claim: All four Igh-J family genes and six Igh-D family genes are used in the IgE repertoire, although IgHD2 dominates.
source: All four Igh-J family genes and six Igh-D family genes were used, although IgHD2 dominated (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data in Figure 2c.

claim: The overall VDJ family gene usage in untreated naïve mice and in the TPA-treated mice is similar.
source: The overall VDJ family gene usage in untreated naïve mice and in the TPA-treated mice was similar (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data in Figure 2b,c.

claim: There are no differences in CDRH3 length, levels of mutation, aliphatic index or isoelectric point between the IgE sequenced from TPA-treated or untreated mice.
source: We found no differences in CDRH3 length, levels of mutation, aliphatic index or isoelectric point (pI) between the IgE sequenced from TPA-treated or untreated mice (Figure 2d), suggesting that the TPA-induced skin inflammation did not alter the composition or the nature of the IgE response.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data in Figure 2d.

claim: The TPA-induced skin inflammation does not alter the composition or the nature of the IgE response.
source: We found no differences in CDRH3 length, levels of mutation, aliphatic index or isoelectric point (pI) between the IgE sequenced from TPA-treated or untreated mice (Figure 2d), suggesting that the TPA-induced skin inflammation did not alter the composition or the nature of the IgE response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequencing data in Figure 2d.

claim: The dominant use of the V1 family and the low mutation rate are consistent with those of 'natural IgE'.
source: The dominant use of the V1 family and the low mutation rate are consistent with those of 'natural IgE' (McCoy et al., 2006), thus we next tested whether the inflammation-induced IgE repertoire contained the characteristic natural anti-phosphorylcholine (anti-PC) (Kearney, 2005) specificity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McCoy et al., 2006.

claim: Skin inflammation enhances the production of anti-PC IgE to a level similar to that of the spontaneous production of natural IgE seen in immunodeficient Tcrb–/– mice.
source: This analysis showed that skin inflammation enhanced the production of anti-PC IgE to a level similar to that of the spontaneous production of natural IgE seen in immunodeficient Tcrb–/– mice (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 2e.

claim: Levels of circulating anti-PC IgE increase further in skin-tumour-bearing mice that have been exposed to TPA for 20 weeks.
source: Levels of circulating anti-PC IgE increased further in skin-tumour-bearing mice that had been exposed to TPA for 20 weeks (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 2e.

claim: Mice lacking IgE (Igh7–/–) are markedly protected from developing tumours in the two-stage DMBA-TPA model.
source: Mice lacking IgE (Igh7–/–) were markedly protected from developing tumours in this two-stage model (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by tumor susceptibility data in Figure 3a.

claim: Igh7–/– mice show an equivalent level of DNA-damage to WT following carcinogen exposure.
source: Although Igh7–/– mice showed an equivalent level of DNA-damage to WT following carcinogen exposure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), as assessed by staining for the phosphorylated histone H2A variant H2AX (γH2AX), only a few Igh7–/– mice developed tumours and the ones that did grew only very few and significantly smaller papillomas (Figure 3a), suggesting that the lack of IgE during TPA promotion hindered tumour growth.
evidence: This is supported by γH2AX staining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Only a few Igh7–/– mice develop tumours and the ones that do grow only very few and significantly smaller papillomas.
source: Although Igh7–/– mice showed an equivalent level of DNA-damage to WT following carcinogen exposure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), as assessed by staining for the phosphorylated histone H2A variant H2AX (γH2AX), only a few Igh7–/– mice developed tumours and the ones that did grew only very few and significantly smaller papillomas (Figure 3a), suggesting that the lack of IgE during TPA promotion hindered tumour growth.
evidence: This is supported by tumor susceptibility data in Figure 3a.

claim: The lack of IgE during TPA promotion hinders tumour growth.
source: Although Igh7–/– mice showed an equivalent level of DNA-damage to WT following carcinogen exposure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), as assessed by staining for the phosphorylated histone H2A variant H2AX (γH2AX), only a few Igh7–/– mice developed tumours and the ones that did grew only very few and significantly smaller papillomas (Figure 3a), suggesting that the lack of IgE during TPA promotion hindered tumour growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tumor data in Figure 3a.

claim: Topical TPA application enhances the circulating levels of IgE in WT animals throughout the DMBA-TPA experiment.
source: The topical TPA application enhanced the circulating levels of IgE in WT animals throughout the experiment (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 3b.

claim: Igh7–/– mice develop no IgE and reduced levels of IgG1 and IgG2a compared to WT animals.
source: Igh7–/– mice developed no IgE and reduced levels of IgG1 and IgG2a compared to WT animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Basophils are the predominant cells carrying IgE in tumours with very few mast cells entering the tumour.
source: Analysis of the tumour tissue and the peri-lesional skin by flow cytometry (Figure 3c) and by qRT-PCR (Figure 3d) showed that basophils were the predominant cells carrying IgE in the tumours with very few mast cells entering the tumour.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 3c and qRT-PCR data in Figure 3d.

claim: The peri-lesional skin contains both mast cells and basophils, whereas mast cells dominate in untreated belly skin.
source: The peri-lesional skin contained both mast cells and basophils, whereas mast cells dominated in untreated belly skin from the same animals (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 3c and qRT-PCR data in Figure 3d.

claim: IgE-bearing cells accumulate right up to the tumour, mainly in the peritumoural infiltrate, with some also entering the epithelium.
source: Cross-sections of whole tumours showed that IgE-bearing cells accumulated right up to the tumour, mainly in the peritumoural infiltrate (Figure 3e), with some also entering the epithelium (Figure 3e inset).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 3e.

claim: TPA causes substantial de novo infiltration of CD45+ leukocytes into the skin, which is equal in WT and Igh7–/– mice.
source: To further explore the role of IgE antibodies during TPA-induced inflammation (the tumour promotion phase), we investigated the skin microenvironment following repeated topical application of TPA on its own to the ear skin. This showed that TPA caused substantial de novo infiltration of CD45+ leukocytes into the skin, which was equal in WT and Igh7–/– mice (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 4a.

claim: There are no substantial differences in the cellular composition of the infiltrates in WT and Igh7–/– mice, aside from a minor increase in dermal Vγ5– γδ T cells.
source: There were no substantial differences in the cellular composition of the infiltrates, aside from a minor increase in dermal Vγ5– γδ T cells, and importantly no difference in mast cell or basophil numbers in either untreated or TPA-treated skin (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: There is no difference in mast cell or basophil numbers in either untreated or TPA-treated skin between WT and Igh7–/– mice.
source: There were no substantial differences in the cellular composition of the infiltrates, aside from a minor increase in dermal Vγ5– γδ T cells, and importantly no difference in mast cell or basophil numbers in either untreated or TPA-treated skin (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: IgE-deficient mice have significantly lower levels of IL-4, IL-5, IL-6 and IL-33 but produce similar levels of TNFα and higher levels of IL-25 transcripts during TPA-induced inflammation.
source: Nevertheless, qRT-PCR analysis of whole skin during TPA-induced inflammation showed that IgE-deficient mice had significantly lower levels of IL-4, IL-5, IL-6 and IL-33 but produced similar levels of TNFα and higher levels of IL-25 transcripts (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4b.

claim: FcεRI+ cells isolated from inflamed skin spontaneously produce some IL-4 and IL-13 protein, which is further increased by IgE crosslinking.
source: In addition, FcεRI+ cells isolated from inflamed skin spontaneously produced some IL-4 and IL-13 protein, and this was further increased by IgE crosslinking (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: A low amount of IL-5 protein is detected from FcεRI+ cells isolated from inflamed skin.
source: A low amount of IL-5 protein was also detected (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: IgE-deficient animals show no enhancement of the enzyme histidine decarboxylase (HDC) responsible for generating histamine.
source: Furthermore, IgE-deficient animals showed no enhancement of the enzyme histidine decarboxylase (HDC) responsible for generating histamine and significantly lower levels of the enzymes involved in the production of bioactive prostanoids such as PGD2 and PGE2 compared to WT mice (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4b.

claim: IgE-deficient animals have significantly lower levels of the enzymes involved in the production of bioactive prostanoids such as PGD2 and PGE2 compared to WT mice.
source: Furthermore, IgE-deficient animals showed no enhancement of the enzyme histidine decarboxylase (HDC) responsible for generating histamine and significantly lower levels of the enzymes involved in the production of bioactive prostanoids such as PGD2 and PGE2 compared to WT mice (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4b.

claim: A significant amount of histamine is released in the inflamed skin of TPA-treated WT mice but not of TPA-treated Igh7–/– mice.
source: Consistent with this, a significant amount of histamine was found to be released in the inflamed skin (Figure 4c) and into the serum (Figure 4d) of TPA-treated WT mice but not of TPA-treated Igh7–/– mice (Figure 4c,d), suggesting that degranulation and histamine discharge was dependent on IgE engagement.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Histamine is released into the serum of TPA-treated WT mice but not of TPA-treated Igh7–/– mice.
source: Consistent with this, a significant amount of histamine was found to be released in the inflamed skin (Figure 4c) and into the serum (Figure 4d) of TPA-treated WT mice but not of TPA-treated Igh7–/– mice (Figure 4c,d), suggesting that degranulation and histamine discharge was dependent on IgE engagement.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Degranulation and histamine discharge is dependent on IgE engagement.
source: Consistent with this, a significant amount of histamine was found to be released in the inflamed skin (Figure 4c) and into the serum (Figure 4d) of TPA-treated WT mice but not of TPA-treated Igh7–/– mice (Figure 4c,d), suggesting that degranulation and histamine discharge was dependent on IgE engagement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the histamine data in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Significantly less epithelial hyperplasia is detected in the absence of IgE during TPA-induced inflammation.
source: Skin analysis by immunohistochemistry also showed obvious changes in TPA-treated inflamed skin in the absence of IgE antibodies. Although both WT and Igh7–/– mice showed a large and equal immune infiltrate in the dermis (Figure 4a,e), significantly less epithelial hyperplasia was detected in the absence of IgE (Figure 4e,f).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining and epidermal thickness measurements in Figure 4e,f.

claim: The lack of IgE substantially alters the skin microenvironment and decreases inflammation-associated epithelial hyperplasia.
source: Together these data demonstrate that the lack of IgE substantially alters the skin microenvironment and decreases inflammation-associated epithelial hyperplasia.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figure 4.

claim: Basophils from TPA-treated skin produce vast amounts of cytokines such as IL-4, IL-6 and IL-13, and are significantly more immune active than mast cells from the same tissue.
source: To determine which cells were primarily responsible for the IgE-mediated exacerbation of skin inflammation, we sorted IgE-bearing mast cells and basophils from TPA-treated skin at a time-point when both cell populations were present. This showed that basophils produced vast amounts of cytokines such as IL-4, IL-6 and IL-13, and that they were significantly more immune active than mast cells from the same tissue (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Basophils sorted from the spleen do not express cytokine transcripts.
source: Basophils sorted from the spleen of the same animal did not express cytokine transcripts (Figure 5b), suggesting that the basophils only became activated when entering the inflamed skin.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5b.

claim: Basophils only become activated when entering the inflamed skin.
source: Basophils sorted from the spleen of the same animal did not express cytokine transcripts (Figure 5b), suggesting that the basophils only became activated when entering the inflamed skin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the qRT-PCR data in Figure 5b.

claim: IgE is partly required to activate basophils for cytokine production when entering the skin.
source: IgE was partly required to activate the basophils for cytokine production when entering the skin (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and IgE-signalling was necessary for degranulation and histamine release because histamine was absent from the skin and serum of both Fcer1a–/– mice (Figure 5c) and Igh7–/– mice (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: IgE-signalling is necessary for degranulation and histamine release.
source: IgE was partly required to activate the basophils for cytokine production when entering the skin (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and IgE-signalling was necessary for degranulation and histamine release because histamine was absent from the skin and serum of both Fcer1a–/– mice (Figure 5c) and Igh7–/– mice (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is supported by histamine ELISA data in Figure 5c and Figure 4c,d.

claim: Histamine is absent from the skin and serum of Fcer1a–/– mice.
source: IgE was partly required to activate the basophils for cytokine production when entering the skin (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and IgE-signalling was necessary for degranulation and histamine release because histamine was absent from the skin and serum of both Fcer1a–/– mice (Figure 5c) and Igh7–/– mice (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is supported by histamine ELISA data in Figure 5c.

claim: Mice with a constitutive depletion of basophils (Mcpt8Cre/+) show a very limited release of histamine in inflamed skin and an absence of histamine in the serum.
source: Indeed, mice with a constitutive depletion of basophils resulting from Cre toxicity (Ohnmacht et al., 2010) (Mcpt8Cre/+) showed a very limited release of histamine in inflamed skin and an absence of histamine in the serum (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by histamine ELISA data in Figure 5c.

claim: Mcpt8Cre/+ mice demonstrate significantly less TPA-induced epithelial hyperplasia compared to WT mice.
source: These mice also demonstrated significantly less TPA-induced epithelial hyperplasia compared to WT mice (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by epidermal thickness measurements in Figure 5d.

claim: Basophil-derived conditioned media induces significant upregulation of Ki67 in epithelial cells.
source: To investigate how IgE-mediated activation of basophils may affect skin EC, neonatal skin EC (keratinocytes) were grown in vitro and at 70% confluency supplemented with media from IgE-activated basophils or media alone as control. Basophil-derived conditioned media induced significant upregulation of Ki67 in EC, downregulation of the basal keratins K5 and K14, and upregulation of the suprabasal keratins K1 and K10 (Figure 5e), suggesting that basophil-released mediators promoted proliferation and upwards differentiation of skin EC.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5e.

claim: Basophil-derived conditioned media induces downregulation of the basal keratins K5 and K14 in epithelial cells.
source: To investigate how IgE-mediated activation of basophils may affect skin EC, neonatal skin EC (keratinocytes) were grown in vitro and at 70% confluency supplemented with media from IgE-activated basophils or media alone as control. Basophil-derived conditioned media induced significant upregulation of Ki67 in EC, downregulation of the basal keratins K5 and K14, and upregulation of the suprabasal keratins K1 and K10 (Figure 5e), suggesting that basophil-released mediators promoted proliferation and upwards differentiation of skin EC.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5e.

claim: Basophil-derived conditioned media induces upregulation of the suprabasal keratins K1 and K10 in epithelial cells.
source: To investigate how IgE-mediated activation of basophils may affect skin EC, neonatal skin EC (keratinocytes) were grown in vitro and at 70% confluency supplemented with media from IgE-activated basophils or media alone as control. Basophil-derived conditioned media induced significant upregulation of Ki67 in EC, downregulation of the basal keratins K5 and K14, and upregulation of the suprabasal keratins K1 and K10 (Figure 5e), suggesting that basophil-released mediators promoted proliferation and upwards differentiation of skin EC.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5e.

claim: Basophil-released mediators promote proliferation and upwards differentiation of skin epithelial cells.
source: To investigate how IgE-mediated activation of basophils may affect skin EC, neonatal skin EC (keratinocytes) were grown in vitro and at 70% confluency supplemented with media from IgE-activated basophils or media alone as control. Basophil-derived conditioned media induced significant upregulation of Ki67 in EC, downregulation of the basal keratins K5 and K14, and upregulation of the suprabasal keratins K1 and K10 (Figure 5e), suggesting that basophil-released mediators promoted proliferation and upwards differentiation of skin EC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the qRT-PCR data in Figure 5e.

claim: Basophil media induces the expression of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1α, IL-18 and IL-31 in epithelial cells.
source: Basophil media also induced the expression of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1α, IL-18 and IL-31 in EC (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Histamine induces expression of Ki67 and suprabasal keratin K1 and reduces expression of K14 in epithelial cells grown in vitro.
source: A similar pattern of induced expression of Ki67 and suprabasal keratin K1 and reduced expression of K14 was demonstrated when EC were grown in vitro with histamine (Figure 5f), and the dose-dependent response to histamine was completely blocked when the EC cultures were pre-incubated with histamine receptor 1 or 4 (H1R or H4R) antagonists (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5f.

claim: The dose-dependent response to histamine is completely blocked when epithelial cell cultures are pre-incubated with H1R or H4R antagonists.
source: A similar pattern of induced expression of Ki67 and suprabasal keratin K1 and reduced expression of K14 was demonstrated when EC were grown in vitro with histamine (Figure 5f), and the dose-dependent response to histamine was completely blocked when the EC cultures were pre-incubated with histamine receptor 1 or 4 (H1R or H4R) antagonists (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5f.

claim: Basophil-induced epithelial cell proliferation and differentiation is partially impeded by H1R or H4R blockade both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Indeed, the basophil-induced EC proliferation and differentiation was also partially impeded by H1R or H4R blockade both in vitro (Figure 5g) and in vivo (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5g and epidermal thickness measurements in Figure 5h.

claim: IgE-signalling in skin-infiltrating basophils directly promotes epithelial cell activation, proliferation and differentiation, partly via the activities of histamine receptors H1R and/or H4R on epithelial cells.
source: Thus, IgE-signalling in skin-infiltrating basophils directly promote EC activation, proliferation and differentiation, partly via the activities of histamine receptors H1R and/or H4R on EC.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figure 5.

claim: Treating mice with pertussis toxin (PTX) prior to topical TPA significantly reduces the recruitment of basophils to the skin.
source: Next, we explored how IgE-bearing basophils are recruited to inflamed skin. Treating mice with pertussis toxin (PTX) prior to topical TPA significantly reduced the recruitment of basophils to the skin (Figure 6a), indicating a role for G-protein-coupled receptors such as chemokine receptors (CCRs) in this process.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 6a.

claim: G-protein-coupled receptors such as chemokine receptors play a role in basophil recruitment to inflamed skin.
source: Next, we explored how IgE-bearing basophils are recruited to inflamed skin. Treating mice with pertussis toxin (PTX) prior to topical TPA significantly reduced the recruitment of basophils to the skin (Figure 6a), indicating a role for G-protein-coupled receptors such as chemokine receptors (CCRs) in this process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PTX blocking data in Figure 6a.

claim: TPA-treated inflamed skin shows increased levels of Ccl2, Ccl5, Ccl8, Ccl11 and Cxcl12 mRNAs when compared with normal untreated skin.
source: In support of this idea, TPA-treated inflamed skin showed increased levels of Ccl2, Ccl5, Ccl8, Ccl11 and Cxcl12 mRNAs when compared with normal UT skin (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6b.

claim: Infiltrating basophils show preferential expression of Cxcr2, Cxcr4 and Ptger2 (CrTH2), which differs significantly from the CCRs expressed on mast cells from the same tissue.
source: In parallel, infiltrating basophils showed preferential expression of Cxcr2, Cxcr4 and Ptger2 (CrTH2 – the PGD2 receptor), which differed significantly from the CCRs expressed on mast cells from the same tissue (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6c.

claim: Blocking CXCR2 with a neutralising antibody inhibits the TPA-induced recruitment of neutrophils but not of basophils.
source: Therefore, we tested the effect of blocking the most abundant chemokine receptors on basophil recruitment to inflamed skin. Blocking CXCR2 with a neutralising antibody inhibited the TPA-induced recruitment of neutrophils but not of basophils (Figure 6d), whereas mice lacking CCR2 (Ccr2–/–) had reduced recruitment of monocytes but not of basophils (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 6d.

claim: Mice lacking CCR2 (Ccr2–/–) have reduced recruitment of monocytes but not of basophils.
source: Therefore, we tested the effect of blocking the most abundant chemokine receptors on basophil recruitment to inflamed skin. Blocking CXCR2 with a neutralising antibody inhibited the TPA-induced recruitment of neutrophils but not of basophils (Figure 6d), whereas mice lacking CCR2 (Ccr2–/–) had reduced recruitment of monocytes but not of basophils (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 6e.

claim: Blocking CXCR4 with a neutralising antibody significantly and selectively reduces basophil infiltration to the inflamed skin.
source: By contrast, blocking CXCR4 with a neutralising antibody significantly and selectively reduced basophil infiltration to the inflamed skin (Figure 6f), suggesting a role for CXCL12-CXCR4 in driving the basophil recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 6f.

claim: CXCL12-CXCR4 plays a role in driving basophil recruitment to inflamed skin.
source: By contrast, blocking CXCR4 with a neutralising antibody significantly and selectively reduced basophil infiltration to the inflamed skin (Figure 6f), suggesting a role for CXCL12-CXCR4 in driving the basophil recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CXCR4 blocking data in Figure 6f.

claim: Resting basophils abundantly express CXCR4, but most of this is intracellular.
source: However, although resting basophils abundantly expressed CXCR4, most of this was intracellular (Figure 6g); therefore, we explored whether any mediators that are released during skin inflammation might upregulate the surface expression of CXCR4 by basophils.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 6g.

claim: Basophils stimulated with TSLP or IL-3 show upregulated expression of CXCR4 on the cell surface.
source: Indeed, basophils that are stimulated with TSLP or IL-3, which are abundantly expressed in inflamed skin (Figure 6h and Dalessandri and Strid, 2014), (or with PMA/ionomycin as a control) showed upregulated expression of CXCR4 on the cell surface (Figure 6i–k).
evidence: This is supported by FACS and Imagestream data in Figure 6i-k.

claim: De novo expression of CXCR4 RNA is induced by TSLP.
source: De novo expression of CXCR4 RNA was induced by TSLP (Figure 6i), and the intracellular pool of CXCR4 protein was transported to the cell surface when basophils were stimulated with TSLP or IL-3 (Figure 6j,k).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 6i.

claim: The intracellular pool of CXCR4 protein is transported to the cell surface when basophils are stimulated with TSLP or IL-3.
source: De novo expression of CXCR4 RNA was induced by TSLP (Figure 6i), and the intracellular pool of CXCR4 protein was transported to the cell surface when basophils were stimulated with TSLP or IL-3 (Figure 6j,k).
evidence: This is supported by FACS and Imagestream data in Figure 6j,k.

claim: There is a complete lack of basophil recruitment to the inflamed skin of mice lacking all T cells.
source: As IL-3 is classically produced by T cells, we next examined the effect of depleting T cells, and found a complete lack of basophil recruitment to the inflamed skin of mice lacking all T cells (Figure 6l).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 6l.

claim: Reducing IL-3 levels during skin inflammation by intradermal injection of neutralising antibodies reduces the recruitment of basophils.
source: In support, we found that reducing IL-3 levels during skin inflammation by intradermal injection of neutralising antibodies also reduced the recruitment of basophils (Figure 6m).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 6m.

claim: Blocking TSLP significantly reduces basophil recruitment to inflamed skin.
source: Similarly, blocking TSLP significantly reduced basophil recruitment to inflamed skin and blocking TSLP and IL-3 simultaneously abolished basophil recruitment (Figure 6m).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 6m.

claim: Blocking TSLP and IL-3 simultaneously abolishes basophil recruitment.
source: Similarly, blocking TSLP significantly reduced basophil recruitment to inflamed skin and blocking TSLP and IL-3 simultaneously abolished basophil recruitment (Figure 6m).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 6m.

claim: Intradermal injection of blocking antibodies in one ear also blocks recruitment into the inflamed skin in the contralateral ear.
source: Injection of blocking antibodies intradermally in one ear also blocked recruitment into the inflamed skin in the contralateral ear (Figure 6n), suggesting that the cytokine(s) were acting systemically and not locally on basophil recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 6n.

claim: TSLP and IL-3 act systemically and not locally on basophil recruitment.
source: Injection of blocking antibodies intradermally in one ear also blocked recruitment into the inflamed skin in the contralateral ear (Figure 6n), suggesting that the cytokine(s) were acting systemically and not locally on basophil recruitment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the contralateral blocking data in Figure 6n.

claim: IL-3/TSLP are not chemotactic themselves but basophils demonstrate chemotaxis towards CXCL12.
source: In vitro experiments showed that IL-3/TSLP were not chemotactic themselves but that basophils demonstrated chemotaxis towards CXCL12 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by transwell chemotaxis data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Production of TSLP and IL-3 in inflamed skin drives the surface expression of CXCR4 on systemic basophils, allowing recruitment to the skin in response to increased levels of CXCL12.
source: Together these data show that production of TSLP and IL-3 in inflamed skin drives the surface expression of CXCR4 on systemic basophils, allowing recruitment to the skin in response to increased levels of CXCL12.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figure 6.

claim: Mice lacking FcεRI (Fcer1a–/–) are significantly less susceptible to tumour development in the two-stage inflammation-driven model.
source: As natural IgE promoted EC growth via FcεRI-signalling in basophils during skin inflammation, we next tested whether a similar mechanism may support skin tumour growth. Using the two-stage inflammation-driven model of epithelial carcinogenesis, we found that mice lacking FcεRI (Fcer1a–/–) were significantly less susceptible to tumour development (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by tumor susceptibility data in Figure 7a.

claim: Only few Fcer1a–/– mice develop any tumours at all and the tumours that grow are very small.
source: Only few mice developed any tumours at all and the tumours that grew were very small (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by tumor susceptibility data in Figure 7a.

claim: The composition of the immune infiltrate in both the perilesional skin and the tumour tissue is overall similar in Fcer1a–/– and WT mice, apart from a minor reduction in neutrophils in the tumours from Fcer1a–/– mice.
source: Nevertheless, the composition of the immune infiltrate in both the perilesional skin and the tumour tissue was overall similar in Fcer1a–/– and WT mice, apart from a minor reduction in neutrophils in the tumours from Fcer1a–/– mice (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 7b.

claim: Mice with substantially diminished FcεRI effector cells (Cpa3Cre/+ mice) are significantly protected from tumour development.
source: Further, mice with substantially diminished FcεRI effector cells, Cpa3Cre/+ mice, were also significantly protected from tumour development (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by tumor susceptibility data in Figure 7c.

claim: Cpa3Cre/+ mice lack all mature skin mast cells as a result of Cre toxicity.
source: Cpa3Cre/+ mice lack all mature skin mast cells as a result of Cre toxicity (Feyerabend et al., 2011) and no mast cells were found in either perilesional skin or tumour tissue (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Feyerabend et al., 2011 and FACS data in Figure 7d.

claim: Cpa3Cre/+ mice have substantially reduced basophil numbers with >90% reduction in inflamed skin and perilesional skin, although basophils are detected in the tumour.
source: However, these mice also have substantially reduced basophil numbers with >90% reduction in inflamed skin and perilesional skin, although basophils were detected in the tumour (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 7d.

claim: Mcpt8Cre/+ mice have normal mast cell numbers but a strongly reduced number of basophils.
source: Owing to the dual effect of the Cpa3Cre on mast cells and basophils , we next used Mcpt8Cre/+ mice, which have normal mast cell numbers but a strongly reduced number of basophils (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 7f.

claim: Mcpt8Cre/+ mice are significantly less susceptible to tumour growth.
source: The Mcpt8Cre/+ mice were again significantly less susceptible to tumour growth (Figure 7e), suggesting that FcεRI-signalling in basophils was responsible for tumour growth.
evidence: This is supported by tumor susceptibility data in Figure 7e.

claim: FcεRI-signalling in basophils is responsible for tumour growth in the inflammation-driven model.
source: The Mcpt8Cre/+ mice were again significantly less susceptible to tumour growth (Figure 7e), suggesting that FcεRI-signalling in basophils was responsible for tumour growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tumor data in Figure 7e.

claim: Adding cetirizine, a H1R blocker, to the drinking water during tumour promotion significantly delays tumour onset and suppresses tumour growth.
source: As signalling via histamine receptors H1R and/or H4R on EC were shown to promote EC proliferation and differentiation during skin inflammation, we then tested whether blocking H1R affected tumour outgrowth. Indeed, adding cetirizine, a H1R blocker, to the drinking water during tumour promotion significantly delayed tumour onset and suppressed tumour growth (Figure 7h).
evidence: This is supported by tumor susceptibility data in Figure 7h.

claim: The inflammation-driven tumour promotion is mediated via FcεRI-signalling in skin-infiltrating basophils, partly via histamine release.
source: Together these data demonstrate that the inflammation-driven tumour promotion is mediated via FcεRI-signalling in skin-infiltrating basophils, partly via histamine release.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figure 7.

claim: IgE-mediated immune surveillance in the skin is most probably dominated by mast cells in healthy skin and during the early-phase response.
source: IgE-mediated immune surveillance in the skin is most probably dominated by mast cells in healthy skin and during the early-phase response (as is immune surveillance in allergic disease), whereas the late-phase response is driven by recruited basophils.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The late-phase response in skin is driven by recruited basophils.
source: IgE-mediated immune surveillance in the skin is most probably dominated by mast cells in healthy skin and during the early-phase response (as is immune surveillance in allergic disease), whereas the late-phase response is driven by recruited basophils.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Basophils are dominant over mast cells in the inflamed skin.
source: In our study, basophils were dominant over mast cells in the inflamed skin, and only basophils appeared to enter the tumours, whilst mast cells remained at the base of the tumours and in the surrounding tissue.
evidence: This is supported by FACS and imaging data in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Only basophils appear to enter the tumours, whilst mast cells remain at the base of the tumours and in the surrounding tissue.
source: In our study, basophils were dominant over mast cells in the inflamed skin, and only basophils appeared to enter the tumours, whilst mast cells remained at the base of the tumours and in the surrounding tissue.
evidence: This is supported by FACS and imaging data in Figure 3.

claim: Epidermal hyperplasia during tissue inflammation is driven by FcεRI-signalling in basophils.
source: Epidermal hyperplasia during tissue inflammation was driven by FcεRI-signalling in basophils, and tumour growth also appeared to be promoted mainly by basophils, although we cannot exclude a role for mast cells because Cpa3Cre/+ mice (which lack mast cells and most basophils) were more protected from carcinogenesis than Mcpt8Cre/+ mice (which have normal mast cell numbers but lack most basophils).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Tumour growth appears to be promoted mainly by basophils.
source: Epidermal hyperplasia during tissue inflammation was driven by FcεRI-signalling in basophils, and tumour growth also appeared to be promoted mainly by basophils, although we cannot exclude a role for mast cells because Cpa3Cre/+ mice (which lack mast cells and most basophils) were more protected from carcinogenesis than Mcpt8Cre/+ mice (which have normal mast cell numbers but lack most basophils).
evidence: This is an inference based on data in Figure 7.

claim: A role for mast cells in tumor promotion cannot be excluded because Cpa3Cre/+ mice were more protected from carcinogenesis than Mcpt8Cre/+ mice.
source: Epidermal hyperplasia during tissue inflammation was driven by FcεRI-signalling in basophils, and tumour growth also appeared to be promoted mainly by basophils, although we cannot exclude a role for mast cells because Cpa3Cre/+ mice (which lack mast cells and most basophils) were more protected from carcinogenesis than Mcpt8Cre/+ mice (which have normal mast cell numbers but lack most basophils).
evidence: This is an inference based on data in Figure 7.

claim: Mast cells have been shown to support SCC growth in tumour models driven by human papilloma virus.
source: Further, mast cells have previously been shown to support SCC growth in tumour models driven by human papilloma virus (Coussens et al., 1999; Bergot et al., 2014) and indeed may contribute to the tumour promotion shown in our study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coussens et al., 1999 and Bergot et al., 2014.

claim: Other skin cancer studies have not found a clear role for mast cells in tumour progression or even shown an anti-tumourogenic role.
source: Nevertheless, other skin cancer studies have not found a clear role for mast cells in tumour progression or even shown an anti-tumourogenic role; thus, the role of mast cells in skin cancer development remain controversial and most probably depends on the underlying factors driving the disease (Varricchi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Varricchi et al., 2017.

claim: The role of mast cells in skin cancer development remains controversial and most probably depends on the underlying factors driving the disease.
source: Nevertheless, other skin cancer studies have not found a clear role for mast cells in tumour progression or even shown an anti-tumourogenic role; thus, the role of mast cells in skin cancer development remain controversial and most probably depends on the underlying factors driving the disease (Varricchi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretive statement supported by citation to Varricchi et al., 2017.

claim: Basophils regulate immunity at many levels, often distinct from mast cells.
source: Although the physiological role of basophils remain poorly understood, it is increasingly recognised that basophils regulate immunity at many levels, often distinct from mast cells (Voehringer, 2013; Karasuyama et al., 2009; Schwartz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Voehringer, 2013; Karasuyama et al., 2009; Schwartz et al., 2016.

claim: Skin-infiltrating basophils, but not mast cells, are crucial for acquired tick resistance in mice.
source: For example, skin-infiltrating basophils, but not mast cells, have been shown to be crucial for acquired tick resistance in mice (Tabakawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tabakawa et al., 2018.

claim: The mechanism of basophil-mediated tick host defence is by epidermal thickening driven by local histamine release.
source: Interestingly, the mechanism of basophil-mediated tick host defence is by epidermal thickening driven by local histamine release (Tabakawa et al., 2018), consistent with the role of basophils and histamine in EC growth demonstrated in our study.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tabakawa et al., 2018.

claim: Histamine has wide-ranging effects on skin epithelial cells and has been shown to promote wound healing in the skin.
source: Histamine has wide-ranging effects on skin ECs and has previously been shown to promote wound healing in the skin (Gutowska-Owsiak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gutowska-Owsiak et al., 2014.

claim: H4R-signalling strongly affects skin epithelial cells.
source: For a long time, the effects of histamine in skin diseases have been thought to be mediated solely by its action on H1Rs, however newer findings, including this report, suggest that H4R-signalling strongly affects skin ECs.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: H4R-deficient mice have thinner epidermis than WT mice at steady state.
source: H4R-deficient mice have thinner epidermis than WT mice at steady state (Glatzer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Glatzer et al., 2013.

claim: H4R-deficiency or blockade significantly reduces epidermal hyperplasia in inflammatory settings.
source: Furthermore, H4R-deficiency or blockade significantly reduces epidermal hyperplasia (Rossbach et al., 2016) and total skin thickness (Cowden et al., 2010) in inflammatory settings.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rossbach et al., 2016 and Cowden et al., 2010.

claim: Mice lacking histidine decarboxylase (HDC) are more susceptible to inflammation-induced carcinogenesis of the skin and colon.
source: Surprisingly, mice lacking histidine decarboxylase (HDC) (the enzyme responsible for histamine generation) are more susceptible to inflammation-induced carcinogenesis of the skin and colon (Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2011.

claim: The increased susceptibility to carcinogenesis in HDC-deficient mice is due to an important role for histamine in myeloid cell differentiation and maturation within the bone marrow.
source: However, this is due to an important role for histamine in myeloid cell differentiation and maturation within the bone marrow (through H1R and H2R), and HDC-deficient mice have significantly altered myeloid cell composition including a large increase in immature myeloid cells, which are recruited to the tissue during inflammation and promote cancer growth (Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2011.

claim: HDC-deficient mice have significantly altered myeloid cell composition including a large increase in immature myeloid cells.
source: However, this is due to an important role for histamine in myeloid cell differentiation and maturation within the bone marrow (through H1R and H2R), and HDC-deficient mice have significantly altered myeloid cell composition including a large increase in immature myeloid cells, which are recruited to the tissue during inflammation and promote cancer growth (Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2011.

claim: Endogenous IgE antibodies that have natural specificities potently affect skin epithelial cell growth and differentiation with implications for both atopy and cancer.
source: Overall, our studies demonstrate how endogenous IgE antibodies that have natural specificities potently affect skin EC growth and differentiation with implications for both atopy and cancer.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claim: The data may have potential important implications for both atopy and cancer.
source: Moreover, our data may have potential important implications for both atopy and cancer.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.
